A_target.statement:
Let $T$ be a [[Definition:Theory (Logic)|theory]] extending [[Definition:Robinson Arithmetic|Robinson arithmetic]].
Let $\map B x$ be a [[Definition:Well-Formed Formula|formula]] with one free variable.
Then there exists a [[Definition:Sentence|sentence]] $G$ such that:
:$T \vdash G \leftrightarrow \map B {\ulcorner G \urcorner}$
where $\ulcorner G \urcorner$ is the [[Definition:Gödel Number|Gödel number]] of $G$.

B_source.statement:
The [[Definition:Liar Paradox|liar sentence]] $L$ is a [[Definition:Sentence|sentence]] built by self-reference which asserts its own falsity:
:$L \leftrightarrow \neg \map {\operatorname {True} } {\ulcorner L \urcorner}$

substitutions.the informal self-reference of the liar: substitution of a term's own code into a formula

derived.the sentence refers to itself: G is provably equivalent to B applied to the code of G
derived.the informal contradiction: a theorem rather than a paradox, because truth is replaced by an arbitrary formula

object_map.reformulation: Replace informal self-reference by substitution of codes, and replace the truth predicate by an arbitrary formula.

validity_conditions: Self-reference is made rigorous by the substitution function, which is representable in the theory; this replaces the informal 'this sentence'.
Because B is an arbitrary formula rather than a truth predicate, the construction produces a theorem instead of a contradiction.
The paradox reappears only if B is taken to be a truth predicate defined inside the theory, which is precisely what Tarski's theorem rules out.
proof_plan:
Let $\operatorname {sub}$ be the function sending $\tuple {\ulcorner \phi \urcorner, n}$ to $\ulcorner \map \phi {\bar n} \urcorner$.
$\operatorname {sub}$ is [[Definition:Primitive Recursive Function|primitive recursive]], hence [[Definition:Representable Function|representable]] in $T$ by a formula $\map S {x, y, z}$.

Given $\map B x$, let:
:$\map D x = \exists z \paren {\map S {x, x, z} \land \map B z}$
which substitutes a code into itself before applying $B$.

Let $G = \map D {\overline {\ulcorner D \urcorner} }$.
Then $\map {\operatorname {sub} } {\ulcorner D \urcorner, \ulcorner D \urcorner} = \ulcorner G \urcorner$.

By representability, $T \vdash \forall z \paren {\map S {\overline {\ulcorner D \urcorner}, \overline {\ulcorner D \urcorner}, z} \leftrightarrow z = \overline {\ulcorner G \urcorner} }$.
Hence:
:$T \vdash G \leftrightarrow \map B {\ulcorner G \urcorner}$
{{qed}}
